subsubtopic: REDUCED SERVICE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stands today to deliver his budget address, I am sure that he will mention the many taxes which he has piled upon Canadians since 1984. Each day workers are taking home less and less money. Canadians are paying more, yet the Government, and especially Canada Post, are cutting their services to those same people.
First it was rural post offices. Now people in the communities in the West Prince area of our province will have their mail delivery cut back. This is unacceptable.
Furthermore, where is the consultation that Canada Post promised? Nobody contacted my office, so I urge the Minister responsible for Canada Post to cancel this decision and restore proper mail service to the people in the western part of Prince Edward Island.

Mr. Speaker, Conservative Member Gabriel Desjardins has come up with a tremendous idea, which is to make Rouyn-Noranda a national environmental research centre which would benefit not only Temis-camingue but also Abitibi.
According to Gabriel Desjardins, his riding has become a national and international laboratory and could be used as an observation centre.
I agree, and I think all of us in Quebec and across Canada should support Mr. Desjardins.

subsubtopic: REPUDIATION OF NEWSPAPER ARTICLE BY FORMER HOUSE SPEAKER FRANCIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Lloyd Francis, former Speaker of this House, is mistaken. His Citizen article "Illegal Immigration Time Bomb in our Society" attacks Canada's 10-year refugee policy based on the United Nations Refugee Treaty we signed 20 years ago.
He does a disservice to Canada by raising irrational fear of refugees with mistaken statements such as these: that for 500 million immigrants and 40 million refugees Canada is a preferred destination-no responsible authority supports such wild exaggeration-and that humanitarian groups seek exemption from the law so as to help illegal immigrants.
What a slander. Of the dozens of witnesses against Bill C-84, not one asked for exemption because all were conscientiously obeying the law by bringing refugee claimants, not illegal immigrants, to Canadian immigration offices.
Does Mr. Francis wish us to ignore refugees persecuted by Governments in some former colonial countries? Canada benefits by the cheap exports of those countries and is partner to some of their violently repressive Governments that enforce virtual slave labour at starvation wages. These refugees Mr. Francis fears are the voice of our conscience.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-STATEMENT ISSUED BY PRESIDENT OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Archbishop James Hayes, President of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement on January 28 on the Supreme Court's decision regarding abortion laws. The following are quotes from that statement:
The situation of "abortion on demand" that follows from the court's decision must be corrected legislatively as soon as possible. This is our common task now, and the future of our human society depends on how soon and how well it is done.
Abortion is the destruction of human life. The challenge is to change our society's attitude toward life and to channel the energies and strong emotions

February 10, 1988

involved in this debate toward correcting mentalities and situations that lead to abortion.
We need to create a society that supports life and enables children to be raised with dignity; a society that puts other people's rights and needs ahead of personal comfort and gain; a society that respects human life at every stage of its development.
The vision and hope that lead us forward flow from our God-given belief that every human life is sacred. Today's Supreme Court decision leaves us in a situation where the sacredness of life is being violated.
We must urgently work together with all Canadians for legislation that will indeed safeguard the life, liberty and security of every person, including the unborn.
May I say Amen to all of that, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR GOOD HOME HEALTH SERVICES PROGRAM FOR SENIORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) on his twenty-fourth anniversary as a Member of the House of Commons. However, I also have a few comments to make about yesterday's statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) concerning senior citizens. I am pleased that the Minister took the advice of the Liberal Party and put back the $5 million he had cut from the New Horizons programs. We agree with the new programs aimed at increasing the autonomy of the elderly, but unfortunately, funding is minimal. We have nearly 2.6 million senior citizens in Canada, and the Government is granting the equivalent of $10 each. Instead of announcing this bare bones program to help senior citizens stay in their own homes, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have set up a full-fledged program of home health care and housekeeping services. That is what they need!

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF NURSES' LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Hon. Members know that Alberta and the City of Calgary will soon be welcoming the world as the Winter Olympics edge closer. In fact, at this very moment, the legendary Olympic Torch is being paraded through my city of Edmonton. All
Canadians are expecting the best Winter Olympics ever. The one potential cloud that looms on the horizon is the nurses' strike currently going on in Alberta.
More than 150,000 people are expected to visit the Olympic site, and although one-quarter of the 9,400 volunteers are trained in First Aid there is nothing like the care of an Alberta nurse to ease one through injury or illness.
Some nurses have shown true western spirit by volunteering their services to the games organizing committee, but picket duty may interfere with their good will, so I call on both the Alberta Hospital Association and the United Nurses of Alberta to settle the dispute quickly. The eyes of the world are upon us.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR EQUAL ACCESS TO SERVICES BY WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court decision on the Morgentaler case found Canada's abortion law unconstitutional in part because therapeutic abortion committees denied women reasonable access, and long delays put women's health in danger. Section 251 of the Criminal Code contravened the Charter which guarantees security of the person.
The federal Government should have provided immediate leadership and should have clearly communicated the implication of this Supreme Court decision. Women must have equal access to abortion across Canada. To deny access to health services, according to the Supreme Court, is to contravene the Charter.
The decision on abortion is a health matter to be decided by a woman in consultation with her doctor. By refusing to take a leadership role immediately, the federal Government has contributed to mass chaos across Canada. Some provinces like British Columbia are victimizing women and imposing impossible decisions on doctors.
We call on the federal Government to instruct the provinces that, under the Canada Health Act, they are responsible for ensuring that medical services are universally accessible, comprehensive, and portable. Health services must be covered by medicare. Women's health clinics with a range of health services should be publicly funded, and the federal Government should immediately launch a campaign in support of family planning to prevent unwanted pregnancies.
February 10, 1988
['Hear, hear!']

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of my Opposition colleagues and of all Canadians to the fact that Question Period has become a real circus. When I was elected, I had to learn about the procedure in the House, and I was told that the main purpose of Question Period was to inform Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, for some time now, we have been exposed to a steady stream of repetitive and harassing questions whose purpose can be only to tarnish the reputation of the Government and all its Members. Mr. Speaker, this is called disinformation and obstruction, and I sincerely believe that the Opposition's role should not consist of those activities.
Mr. Speaker, I think you have a duty to put an end to this charade, otherwise the Canadian people will no longer have access to the information they have a right to receive.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX REFORM ON INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, TIAC, is the country's largest and most important tourism association with a membership covering approximately 30,000 tourism businesses. Recently, TIAC wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) accusing his Government of total disregard for the concerns of the tourism industry in the tax reform legislation.
The Tourism Association stated that if tax reform in Canada places our tourism products and services at a greater competitive disadvantage with the U.S., both our foreign exchange earnings and job-creation potential within Canada will be seriously compromised. The association points out that the Conference Board of Canada is already predicting that the travel account balance of payments deficit for Canada will grow to the $3 billion range by 1990.
If this deficit is allowed to escalate further, it will end up having serious negative employment implications for Canada. In support of TIAC, I urge the Government to start paying attention to our tourism industry. Tourism means jobs, jobs, jobs.
Oral Questions THE BUDGET

Mr. Speaker, I want to help all Canadians understand what the two opposition Leaders will be saying after tonight's Budget. This is what they said the last three times. The Liberal Leader (Mr. Turner) said that "the Budget does not have an economic plan, no agenda for growth and no agenda for jobs''. He was wrong, wrong, wrong.
The NDP Leader (Mr. Broadbent) said that "not only have we had no improvement but things have gotten worse". He was wrong, wrong, wrong.
The Liberal Leader: "There is nothing in it for farmers". No Government has done more for farmers than this Government, and he was wrong again.
On unemployment the NDP Leader said: "The projections show virtually no change". How wrong could that wrong man be?
Bill told me, Mr. Speaker, that after tonight's budget speech he was going to celebrate. He said that Mike Wilson has brought more economic growth, more employment, more real stability, than ever thought possible, and Mike has been constantly right, right, right!
Hear, hear!

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PROVINCIAL COMPLIANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, in testifying before a U.S. congressional committee,

February 10, 1988
Oral Questions
Secretary of the Treasury Baker said that the U.S. will seek compensation or redress from Canada if any provinces do not comply with the terms of the agreement initialled by the Prime Minister and President Reagan. We already know three provinces have said they are not in agreement with the deal.
Can the Prime Minister tell us if the U.S. has the right to seek compensation and redress under the terms of the agreement? As well, is he ready to offer such compensation in view of provincial non-compliance? In other words, is he prepared to give away even more in order to get the deal approved?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PROVINCIAL COMPLIANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously when one concludes a treaty with a trading partner, that partner is quite entitled to assume that the treaty will be fully honoured by the sovereign nation with which it was concluded. That is the assumption under which Mr. Baker is functioning and it is not an inaccurate one.
With regard to the questions raised by my hon. friend, clearly he has not been listening to comments made yesterday by U.S. Congressmen and Senators, many of whom are voicing grave misgivings in regard to the treaty, not because they disagree with the principles involved but because they feel Canada got by far the better deal.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PROVINCIAL COMPLIANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I submit that the Prime Minister did not answer what was a very important question, that is, to what extent does the agreement bind the provinces, to what degree must they comply, and does the U.S. have the right to compensation?

Mr. Speaker, several months ago, under the Freedom of Information Act, we sought from the Department of Justice and other government Departments the legal view of the constitutionality of the agreement and its impact upon the provinces. We got back three blank pages, one with the title of a U.S. law firm, one article from a U.S. trade publication-
Question!

-and an article from The Toronto Star.
Is this the kind of information the Government is working from, and why is it refusing to give parliamentarians and other Canadians a proper legal interpretation of the agreement rather than a bunch of hopeless articles from a U.S. law firm?

Mr. Speaker, surely my hon. friend is not calling into question the sovereign right of the Government of Canada to conclude international treaties and cause them to be enacted. If my hon. friend is stating that as policy of the Liberal Party of Canada, he should stand up in the House and say so.
The Government of Canada, on behalf of the people of Canada, has concluded an international treaty. We believe it is very much in the national interest. We will submit it to
Parliament at an appropriate time and we will ensure that that treaty is respected, as I am sure my hon. friend wants to ensure the respect of all of our international obligations.

As a gentleman who at one time practised law the Prime Minister will know that there was a decision in 1935 on the International Labour Organization which gives the provinces the right not to ratify international agreements signed by the federal Government. For him to try to mislead this House by suggesting-
Order!

speechtext: Order.

If anyone chooses to invoke a challenge, then he, she, or that Government is entirely free to do so and to address the appropriate courts. The Supreme Court of Canada will, no doubt, at an appropriate time, render a decision in this regard.
With regard to the Government, we are absolutely persuaded that we are acting not only within the purview of our legislative authority but very much in the national interest.

subsubtopic: LUBICON BAND LAND CLAIM-NORTHERN ALBERTA PULP MILL PROJECT-TIMBER RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. As the Minister will know, on Monday Premier Getty announced plans for an untendered transfer of harvesting rights to the Daishowa pulp project, some 11,000 square miles of northern Alberta, which is an area over 100 times the size of the area sought by the Lubicon Band for settlement.
Since parts of these lands that were announced on Monday are those sought by the Lubicon Band and, we must assume, by Crown Canada, as the basis for the settlement of the outstanding Lubicon claim, has the Minister expressed concern to the Government of Alberta about the proposed transfer of these lands and the fact that it will be harmful to a peaceful and just settlement of the Lubicon claim?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: LUBICON BAND LAND CLAIM-NORTHERN ALBERTA PULP MILL PROJECT-TIMBER RIGHTS

Mr. Speaker, the way the announcement was made yesterday in Alberta on the transfer of forestry management to assist in the development of a large scale pulp plant in northern Alberta was indeed unnecessary and unhelpful. I can assure the Hon. Member that the 25 square miles originally put forward by Alberta in 1940 have been excluded from that forestry management, and any lands that will be transferred to Canada to settle that outstanding claim, as is Alberta's obligation, will be transferred and exempted from the forestry management agreement between Daishowa and the Province of Alberta.

subsubtopic: BRITISH PLANS TO LABEL FUR PRODUCTS-EFFECT ON LIVELIHOOD OF CANADIAN TRAPPERS

The House resumed from Friday, February 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-105, an Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Mr. Speaker, the occasion of a Railway Safety Act is an important and momentous one in the House of Commons and for the country. We should always remember that rail transportation was one of the keys to creating this confederation. It was created by a commitment to tie together our country with a band of steel which is symbolically, what was the railway. It was an east-west commitment to create a nation in the northern half of this hemisphere.
I think when we deal with revisions to the legislation affecting railways we should always keep in mind that the railway is a part of the vision of this country. I like to remember that when arguments are made about rationalizing, downsizing and elimination of overlapping and duplication. Certainly those are important goals and I am not suggesting that we do the opposite, but we would not have a country if we had not been prepared to do something that seemed pretty irrational at the time, that is to establish a nation on an east-west axis.
We now have before us in Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. As my colleagues indicated, particularly the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud), our principal spokesman on this subject, we support the Bill in principle and are going to vote for it. However, it would be a great deal easier to do so if we knew the Government was prepared to be more flexible than it has so far indicated it intends to be when the Bill moves into committee.
I want to take some time to talk about our specific concerns and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister
himself might respond and indicate that at least some effort will be made to look into the important arguments we on this side have raised because we think that is necessary if the Bill is really to serve the railways and our country.
Just before getting to my main points, I have had some interest in a specific issue of railway safety which I have raised both in the House in Question Period and outside the House through statements and press releases. That concern relates to the transportation of dangerous goods by rail through Metropolitan Toronto. That is a subject dealt with by the Railway Safety Act.
Members should know that this is a matter of great concern for us in Toronto, as it is in western Canada because of the Hinton disaster. For us it was fortunately not a disaster but a very near miss when, several years ago in Mississauga, a train carrying deadly chemicals was nearly derailed. It forced us to confront the issue of the carriage of dangerous goods through Toronto, the location of our rail lines in metropolitan areas, and to reflect on emergency relief and emergency measures when dealing with this type of disaster. It was all hypothetical, thank God, because actual disaster was averted and in the end no one suffered injury. However, it showed us how vulnerable we are to potential disasters which arise from carrying dangerous goods by rail through built-up areas.
When I heard, for example, a couple of years ago that notice was being given by the railways of their intention to close down some important lines running through northern Ontario I could not help but think of the impact that could have on dangerous goods which might be channelled through cities and urban areas because of the shutting down of those lines. That is a powerful argument for keeping lines open outside of urban areas.
I have done some work on statistics and it turns out that most of the dangerous goods carried by rail through dense metropolitan areas are carried to destinations inside those areas. Obviously, for most of them, it is inevitable that they are going to be carried on those lines and the question of northern lines or remote lines is irrelevant. However, the problem of those goods not destined for downtown urban areas or metropolitan areas being carried through those areas if the northern lines are closed down is a problem worth considering.
I want to hear from the Government that it cares about that, and that when the viability of northern lines is being looked at, one of the principal factors which should be considered is that those lines present a method of diverting some dangerous goods from being carried through urban areas.
To those of us, like myself, who represent urban populations, it is important to make that point and it is important to hear from the Government that the point has registered and indeed the northern lines are recognized as a method of diverting dangerous goods, in cases where it is appropriate, from being carried through urban areas.

February 10, 1988

Of course, that is not the only recourse for dealing with dangerous goods. There was a task force meeting in Toronto, I believe it has now concluded its public hearings, which attracted a great deal of interest. It demonstrated a concern that Canadians feel about the problem.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), appeared before that committee and set out a number of ways of providing greater safety when it is inevitable and necessary that dangerous goods be carried to and through urban areas. In his brief he talked about, as he has in this House, a lower speed limit because of the strong likelihood that more care can be taken and more notice of danger given when railway cars are travelling at a lower rate of speed.
He talked about the importance of observation of the cars and the rails. While all kinds of technical methods are available for observation and security and these methods should be used, human observation is an essential part of a proper system of safeguards. People can spot rail defects, loose freight, poisonous leaks, track wash-outs and, perhaps most important, are able to stop the train if an emergency is perceived. These are important and essential safeguards when dangerous goods are carried through areas where people live. He emphasized as well, as I have done now, the importance of lowering the risk in general in heavily-populated areas. That is where, of course, any disaster would have its greatest impact.
In conclusion, I want to turn to the features of the Act that concern us. I know Members opposite are listening with intense interest and I hope they will indicate that these concerns matter and that the Minister will look with some sympathy at these ideas. We are first concerned that a sort of conflict of interest exists in a broad sense for the Minister in assuming some of the powers to be awarded under this Bill when added to his already significant powers; for example, responsibility for deregulation.
The goal of deregulation is simple, to reduce the amount of control by the state over the subject matter, in this case railway carriage. The new or reinforced responsibility awarded by this Act for safety could lead him in the opposite direction, and I would not like to think that the interests of deregulation would be a goal that the Minister would keep in mind when issues of safety are being considered. We know that railways want to operate in an efficient manner and they certainly want to operate in a safe manner. However, regulation has a role to play in assuring that they do operate in a safe manner. [DOT]
We would like to hear that the Minister is not obsessed with the goal of deregulation and that that will not be a consideration which prevents him from considering the kind of regulations which I have urged in my remarks today and that others have urged when these disasters have arisen and when the problems of safe passage have been considered.
Railway Safety Act
Second, my colleagues have made the point that the fines and penalties provided for in Clause 41 do not give enough range to a court. I am not saying that the amounts are not substantial and that they may not cover most of the situations in which penalties will be imposed. However, when you think of the seriousness of the consequences of some unsafe procedures for which fines may be imposed, a maximum fine of $50,000 to a corporation and $10,000 to an individual seems small.
One could imagine the situation in a corporate boardroom of a decision being made when a very expensive regulation or costly procedure is being considered. Although they will be careful and try to avoid doing anything wrong or getting caught, if they are caught $50,000 is a lot less than it would cost to avoid the problem. Much larger fines would be in order in the circumstances of the risks and costs of implementing regulations about which we are speaking here.
Third, I want to talk about the committee which is proposed to be set up pursuant to Clause 44. That committee is to be composed, according to the draft legislation, of one position for labour, six for businesses and the railways, and four at the Minister's discretion. I do not think that is a fair balance. I think it would be better to provide more representation from labour if there is to be that much representation from business and railways.
I am not only thinking of labour from the point of view of issues of labour management or the point of view of workers' concerns as workers. Some of the most expert people on the subject of rail transportation and safety are people who have hands-on experience, who know how trains operate, and who know the kinds of situations which can arise. Therefore, I say that not only from the point of view that business and labour have a different perspective, but from the point of view of having someone who knows how railways work from a hands-on position. I hope that the Government will concede that more than one labour voice be put on the committee by right, and not just if the Minister feels like it, as is the present provision of the Bill.
Also, there ought to be an official designation of one position on such a committee for a community representative. Who the community representative should be would depend on the circumstances. It could be a designate of the mayor or council of a community. It could be someone in a ratepayers' association when a smaller issue is at stake which only affects that kind of a limited group. It could perhaps be someone from a consumer group who would want to bring to bear the position of consumers.
However, to say that if the Minister so chooses the committee could operate without such a person is overlooking one of the sources of legitimacy which we want such a committee to have and the respect which we want the public to give to the decisions which such a committee reaches.
A fourth area of concern has to do with the hours of work which will be applied in circumstances where rail safety is

February 10, 1988
Railway Safety Act
being considered. I would like the statute itself to lay out some guidelines. The Parliament of Canada should indicate in legislation some type of scheduling to give a signal about the standards which we want to apply to those who work on the railways and whose attention and energy are affected by long hours of work or too much overtime on particular shifts over a long period of time. Parliament ought to do a bit more than identify that as an issue and leave it totally to be established outside the legislation.
We want this Bill to move forward.

It is a significant undertaking. We must always make progress in the field of railroad safety. We are very much in favour of that, and we hope that the contribution we are making now in terms of ideas and suggestions will be of some interest to the Government.

Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker dealt very effectively with some of the key issues on this matter. I wonder whether he would be in a position to elaborate in a little more detail on shortcomings arising from the Mississauga event regarding hazardous products. There have been a number of serious incidents subsequent to that. Has he any additional concerns about sufficient prevention in the carriage of dangerous products?

Mr. Speaker, 1 could go on at great length on this subject. I have in my office the report on the incident which I have read with great interest and also the work of the task force which has just concluded. 1 know the Hon. Member is as concerned as I am about railway safety. I want to ensure that he receives a copy of the report. From that he will see what this task force, which was appointed by a Conservative Government but seems to be doing a very good job, is going to propose.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member with great interest and I appreciate the remarks he made about the transportation of dangerous goods. Does he realize that in a metropolitan area such as Toronto thousands of tonnes of dangerous goods move every day to and from manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, and processors? If we were to move rail lines further out of Toronto those same dangerous goods would have to move by road through Metropolitan Toronto. As the Member, I, and everyone else all know, the incident of accidents on the road, particularly involving trucks, is many times higher than on the rails. Despite the Mississauga incident, rail is still the safest way to go.
Does the Hon. Member think that that consideration should override the demand for the wholesale moving of railway tracks, whether spur tracks into warehouses or mainline tracks, out of a metropolitan area?

Mr. Speaker, my friend makes a very good point. I agree with him that rail carriage is perhaps the safest way of transporting dangerous goods. The wholesale removal of lines from urban areas where they are needed, with the objective of forcing the transportation of these goods on to the roads, is no real solution. It is a step backward.
The first priority is to be certain that rail lines within urban areas are not being used to carry dangerous goods that are irrelevant to the economy of that community. If the line is being used simply because it is the shortest distance between two points, through what happens to be a great metropolitan centre, a high priority should be given to a diversion of that commodity to a railway line that goes around the city,
Art Eggleton, the Mayor of Toronto, made an impassioned plea before the task force on the transport of dangerous goods, to urge them to build a new line going around the city. It would cost some $700 million to build a line so that goods would not have to go through the city unnecessarily. While that is a very substantial amount of money, it can be less than the cost of a disaster that could occur.
Furthermore, such a line could be used to move goods from one side of the city to the other, thereby increasing the safety of the population in the urban area by moving goods around the city on a rail line rather than through. When one adds all these elements to the equation, it is evident that a line like that could be a very important factor in making our urban areas a safer place for residents.
Finally, there is the question of dangerous goods that are required in the cities. Historically, certain industries that require the use of dangerous goods have been in the hearts of our cities. It may be worth giving some priority to the thought of relocating those industries to industrial suburbs where many of the risks that are involved might be reduced.
I once visited the site of a former bomb factory in New Brunswick. I was given a long explanation about the measures that had been taken to divide the operation into a number of buildings and caves on this vast site in an effort to make them as safe as possible. One might suggest that that type of planning could be done in the first place when dangerous goods are involved in industrial projects, but I do not want to rebuild our cities around this principle. We should keep that in mind in everything we do as a Parliament, and governments as well at other levels. We should take account of the increasing danger of these industrial activities and try to make them truly as safe as possible.

Mr. Speaker, many people are concerned that this Bill will allow the railways to make their own rules to an even greater extent than they have in the past, and that the decision about how to care for such things as the movement of dangerous goods may be tied to economic considerations. Will the Hon. Member suggest an alternative to this method of
February 10, 1988

ensuring that the rules that are put in place by the railways will provide safety in the movement of those kinds of goods?

Mr. Speaker, the safety function which I mentioned earlier and said should not reside with the Minister to the extent it does, perhaps could be given to the safety board that is also referred to in the legislation. At least the safety board has as its main concern the question of safety.

If we consider that the Minister wants deregulation and is actively promoting this issue, whenever he has to come to grips with safety problems he may be prepared to compromise to achieve deregulation or give it first priority.
Given the safety plan now being proposed, why not give more power to this agency so it will feel free to make any decision aimed at ensuring maximum safety without compromising in respect of deregulation issues.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. It has already been pointed out that the New Democratic Party supports the legislation in principle since anything that will lead to a safer transportation environment is to the benefit of all Canadians.
My main area of concern is the political will of the Government to deal effectively with questions of safety. We know that the legislation on rail safety is likely only before the House today as a result of four wrecks that occurred during the last month. There were wrecks in London, Sudbury and Regina where two people lost their lives. The Bill arises only because of the crisis management nature of the Government rather than a timely and organized approach toward enhancing transportation safety.
This is a reflection of a general problem with the Government. On the one hand it expresses its serious concern about certain problems, while on the other hand it tends to delay implementation of legislation which, from a philosophical point of view, erodes its effectiveness.
We have heard for some time a litany of concerns about rail equipment safety, timely upgrading and proper inspection of that equipment. We have heard about railway grades that need substantial improvement and repair because they eventually become a serious hazard to safety.
The transportation of dangerous goods is of great concern. Cars containing propane have overturned, and dangerous chemicals have been spilled. Many Canadians believe that the attempt to address the problem of the transport of dangerous goods, especially in sensitive areas, has been inadequate. In the last several years the injuries, loss of life and the destruction of property have increased our concern about rail safety. In the last year some 350 people were killed at level crossings, of which there are thousands in Canada. Most of the level crossings in Europe disappeared years ago. However, this
Railway Safety Act
country's penny wise and pound foolish approach to railway transportation safety has not allowed us to effectively deal with the problem of level railway crossings.
Urban centres like Vancouver, Mississauga and Toronto must face the safety aspect of dangerous goods transported by rail every day.
The double tracking of the Fraser Canyon is of great concern to us. Just over a year ago the Fisheries and Oceans Committee heard serious concerns about the intention of the double tracking of the CN through that very delicate environment where slides and the disturbance of the local ecology have the potential of serious environmental impact. Other concerns include the danger to the goods that are transported and the problems associated with that. As well, there are the concerns of aboriginal people. We are very concerned about the double tracking proposal and, later on in the future, the possibility of the double tracking of sections of the other carrier through the Fraser Canyon.
It is quite surprising that the Government and the railways seem to again choose the penny wise and pound foolish route of dealing with the problem rather than considering the many other safer alternatives that were proposed. But the Government chose not to insist that the railways explore those possibilities and take the pressure off that sensitive environmental area. The cheapest way is the best way in the minds of some people in this present Government.
Another serious concern we have involves the whole question of the integrity of the safety infrastructure. Over a period of time there has been a profound feeling that although the Government is saying it is very concerned about safety, there is an erosion of the will of Government to become aggressive and active on safety issues. We would point out that the deregulation program of this Government is bound to create more safety problems than it will resolve. The experience in the United States tends to indicate that as the deregulation process goes into place, major safety problems arise.
There is the whole question of the aviation industry. We have seen a massive expansion of aviation activity, by way of comparison. Both the growing economy and the deregulated environment have resulted in a massive increase in air transportation traffic. At the same time, the Government has failed to apply adequate human resources for inspection, safety compliance operations and accident investigation. The application of these human resources has not been expanded to keep up with the expansion of activity. On the other hand, the Public Service has gone through a number of cuts which has led to intense pressure on those responsible for inspection and investigation and who deal with questions of safety.
Therefore, deregulation has had an impact on expanding activity, along with an improved economy, since the days of the early 1980s. Yet at the same time the Government has gone in absolutely the opposite direction and laid off public

February 10, 1988
Railway Safety Act
servants, allowed the Public Service to shrink by attrition, and essentially loaded more and more responsibilities onto a smaller and smaller group of people who, in fact, cannot handle, other than through a very low-grade spot-check system, the safety factor. As we watch more and more carriers operating and more and more activity because of economic growth, we will find that those people are certainly not going to be able to guarantee the integrity of the safety infrastructure.
On the question of the lack of the Government's will to continue to strengthen the safety infrastructure, we have the problem of the removal of resources. The people who are still in the system, doing the inspections, the safety enforcement, prevention and accident investigation, are finding that because of the Government's desire to curtail deficits, to reduce overall spending, there are fewer and fewer resources to do a decent job and guarantee to the public that its safety is a matter of priority and is being looked after in an effective and timely manner.
The Government's will to develop and enhance the safety system in Canada, therefore, is being harmed by its budgetary activities. The cuts to spending, the inability to obtain adequate resources to do the kinds of things that can guarantee safety, is apparent to most Canadians.
Again, it is a matter of serious concern to us. Over all, the Government's philosophy almost contradicts its stated intention to improve safety. In a deregulated environment, the Government wants to remove itself from the back of business and basically say, "You get out there and do it. You are responsible for safety and we are counting on you to undertake the problem". We see the Conservative philosophy of getting Government off the back of business as almost a contradiction to improvement in safety.
Secondly, there is a lack of political will in enforcing safety regulations. We have a situation in which there is Government interference, where there have been Public Service attempts to enforce safety regulations, and where those attempts on occasion have been modified by direct interference by Government. Even though regulation may be there, the question of the will to enforce those regulations on the part of the Government is a matter of serious question. I have gone into the whole question of Public Service staff and financial resources at great length. Each year, with growing traffic problems and with the growing number of people involved in the business, we wind up with a situation where those resources are far too inadequate to deal with the problem.
It is interesting to note that on this issue of resolve in the safety area, the Ministry of Transport has quite a negative track record. I would point to the issue of the lighthouses. The Department of Transport is charged not only with railway safety but with marine and air safety. In the marine environment, by way of example, the Government had intended to shut down a majority of the lighthouses on the coast of British Columbia. In the face of a massive amount of evidence that
those lighthouses were providing a very important safety network along the coast of British Columbia, the Government charged ahead with its objective to shut those facilities down. It was clearly demonstrated that they needed to be enhanced. There is a need for improved weather reporting capability and communication equipment; indeed, there is a need for the human resources to do the job.
But the Government was completely unwilling to upgrade that structure even though marine transportation was increasing along the coast of British Columbia, and even though there are a substantial number of serious accidents every year, and lighthouse keepers have played an important role in mediating those accidents. Yet the Government preferred to move in the other direction, to cut human and financial resources, saying, "It is not our mandate", which is a very curious thing. In dealing with the over-all responsibility of transportation, whether it be commercial, recreational or tourist transportation, that Department is saying that giving weather forecast to those vessels is not its responsibility, but the responsibility of some other Government Department, so it is going to chop it. Indeed, a very narrow, short-sighted approach to marine safety is illustrated by the Government's desire to cut those lighthouses.
It was pointed out by a previous'speaker that over the years there has been an interesting conflict of interest in enforcing safety. The Minister of Transport has a dual role in many cases, especially under the new transportation legislation, to deregulate the environment, to encourage more carriers and to facilitate their opportunity to become involved in the industry. At the same time, there is a deterrent and expensive proposition to enforce rigorous safety standards. At times the Minister comes into a conflict situation.
To move over to the air side, to illustrate this point as it would apply to rail safety, we see it as an awkward area that we are certainly loading onto the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and onto the Ministry, away from the Canadian Transport Commission. Instead of an organization that operates to some degree at arm's length from the Minister, an organization which can, with some objectivity, with independent resources and decisions, apply those resources to prevention, investigation and inspection programs, we now have it locked within the responsibility of the Minister whose mandate is to promote, improve and encourage expansion, and on the other hand, to impose major cost and regulatory burdens in terms of safety.
The Dubin Royal Commission into air safety uncovered this conflict within the aviation branch of the Department of Transport. There is no doubt that that conflict and the requirement to enforce rigorous safety standards within the aviation branch during the period of the Liberal Government wound the Minister of Transport or the Department of Transport into a major conflict.
February 10, 1988

There was political interference in the outcome of many accident investigations. Those people within the safety and accident investigation branches were hampered from bringing their material to public knowledge and to those agencies that could improve the situation, and to impose the burden effectively on the carriers.
We wound up with a Royal Commission, and Judge Dubin stated that these ought to be split off in order that they can function independently, and guarantee to Canadians that air transportation will be as safe as humanly possible, and that that can be done by an outside agency through the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, rather than under the direct auspices of the Minister of Transport.
It was pointed out by the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) that we are moving railway safety into a potential conflict of interest area. That is a matter of concern, given the history dealt with in the Dubin Royal Commission in the early 1980 period.
There is an interesting point in the legislation on penalties. How serious are we about railway safety and the implementation of safety standards, when one considers that an individual can be fined $10,000, yet a corporation can be fined a maximum of $50,000? It is a very strange situation when a manager within the railway system, concerned enough about the Budget for his or her department, can say, "If we are detected for having a faulty system in place, the fine is cheaper than the cost of changing or repairing that situation". With some of the equipment and systems that we are dealing with, $50,000 is an absolute drop in the bucket.
I have spoken with many engineers who are responsible for air safety from a maintenance point of view. They state that indeed the deregulated environment has put pressure on certain air carriers. Years ago a defective part would be taken out and thrown away and another one would be put in. Today that is not done. The part is taken out, fixed up, haywired together in order that it works. It is stuffed back in the machine and they hope for the best. I have heard people say that their hands shakes when they sign the log book stating that that beast is airworthy.
The same situation applies when a safety or maintenance supervisor or a manager states, "We are going overboard on our accounts or budget. What we should do, because this thing probably has a few more hours left in it, is use it". The same thing applies in the railway safety area. There should be penalties in this legislation that are serious deterrents to managers who put the corporation's budget ahead of safety matters.
Within the House there should be serious consideration, especially in committee, to recommending much stronger penalties from a corporate point of view where matters of corporate budget concern exceed the need for safety, where one could find a manager who states, "In order to keep the budget that has been assigned to my department within limits, I am going to overlook the safety requirements here". That is well within the realm of possibility, and there are examples that that is indeed happening today.
Railway Safety Act
In the transportation system the Government got involved in a number of things. The commitment to remove the regulatory burden and the burden of government from the industry, and to some degree from safety, the cutting of human and financial resources to the government department responsible over-all for the implementation of safety, are serious matters. Even in the cost recovery program the example of substantial increases in charts, in navigational material within transport, and down the road the use of Transport Canada services designed to assist in safety imposing a cost to the public or to the users, instead of a general burden to the population, will result in people avoiding the use of those services, taking a chance, and returning us to the old concept of the wild west approach to public safety.
In some areas, the Government has done a major disservice to people by the philosophy that it has imposed on the safety infrastructure of the railway transportation system.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his speech. Earlier in his speech there were actually some remarks directed toward rail safety. The rest of his speech was off the subject of the Bill. I did notice when speaking about rail safety, the Hon. Member gave some attention to the need for double tracking in the Fraser Canyon. I take it from the context of his remarks that he was promoting that idea in order to promote rail safety in the Fraser Canyon. The Hon. Member mentioned when he was on the fisheries committee that he faced a lot of concern about the environment when dealing with the subject of double tracking.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) if he supports double tracking of the Fraser Canyon, or does he not?

I thank the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) for his intervention. Certainly, he must have been wandering a little during the discussion. He knows as clearly as anyone else in the House and in the country the position of the New Democratic Party on double tracking in the Fraser Canyon. The position is clearly stated on the record.
I do wish to deal with another matter that I know is of concern to the Hon. Member-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Are you for or against? Which track are you on?

-that is on the question of drug and alcohol within the legislation. It is interesting that the legislation deals with punitive aspects regarding individuals who are involved in drug an alcohol problems in the workforce. Certainly, it is our hope that under this legislation the Government and the Department of National Health and Welfare will work with the railroads and the railroad employees to see that ideal programs involved in prevention and resolution of personal problems with employees will be undertaken before there are accidents, not simply the old standard of drug testing and the firing of an employee who has contravened the legislation.

February 10, 1988
The Budget-Hon. Michael Wilson
Perhaps, the Government will take the example of the Canadian Armed Forces in relation to alcohol treatment. The Canadian Armed Forces has to be considered one of the leaders in developing treatment programs and rehabilitation programs for its employees. It provides a service to the employee in terms of alcohol and drug rehabilitation that can return the individual to useful and productive service, can remove the problems that are experienced by an employee's family, and the potential risks in a very delicate and serious work situation where the abuse of alcohol and drugs, or personal stress experienced by an individual, can lead to a major safety problem. Of course, this applies to air, marine, and rail safety, and in the Armed Forces these come together in an even more crucial area. That branch has become one of the leaders in Canadian society in the alcohol and drug rehabilitation system.
It is my hope that the provisions that are in this legislation will not be used as a punitive sanction, but to lay down an example in Canada of how employers in the industrial, and especially in the transportation environment, can provide support services to their employees that aim at rehabilitation and returning the individual to the workforce and in particular, preventing the types of accidents and difficult situations that can occur before they happen by recognition and effective treatment and rehabilitation.
I am appreciative of the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta for bringing this matter to the attention of the House in the skilful and effective way he always does. Incidentally, we are also opposed to the double tracking of the CN through the Fraser Canyon.
